name: rapidyaml (ryml)
workload: Parsing/emitting a real-world travis.yml YAML file and a compile_commands.json file, measuring MB/s, comparing ryml against yaml-cpp, libyaml, and libfyaml (bm/bm_parse.cpp, bm/bm_emit.cpp)
claimed_speedup: ~200 MB/s parse / ~600+ MB/s emit; 'generally 30x (parse) / 150x (emit) faster than yamlcpp, and never less than 10x (parse) / 50x (emit)'; raw travis.yml parse data shows ryml up to 30.66x vs yaml-cpp's 1.00x baseline and libyaml only reaching 7.41x vs the same yaml-cpp baseline (derived from page data, i.e. ryml is also several times faster than libyaml on this file)
compiler_and_flags: Release build via CI (Travis/AppVeyor); current docs cite GCC 16.1 / Visual Studio 2026 for the general build matrix, but the exact compiler/flags used for the archived 0.16.0-pre benchmark run are not stated
hardware: Not stated (Travis CI / AppVeyor cloud runners; no CPU model given anywhere in the README or the linked raw results file)
stars_or_usage: 756 stars; used by Google (jsonnet), NVIDIA, CERN (ROOT/LHCb), OpenTelemetry C++, Toyota Research Institute
tradeoffs: Parses into a flat, index-based tree of string views into the source buffer rather than a DOM with owned strings; in-place parsing mutates the source buffer; C++11, deliberately avoids std containers in its own data structures
caveats: Benchmark numbers come from the project's own CI (Travis/AppVeyor) results archived in a separate rapidyaml-data repo; CPU model is never stated, so per the evidence-tier rules this is capped at C (first-party benchmark with partial methodology) despite having public, runnable benchmark code and multiple independently-reported success stories (rATHENA, OpenXcom, CERN LHCb merge request) corroborating large real-world speedups
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "yaml" language:C++ --sort stars (biojppm/rapidyaml)

name: fkYAML
workload: Parsing ubuntu.yml, citm_catalog.json, and citm_catalog.yml, measuring processed bytes/sec in Release mode with Google Benchmark, comparing fkYAML against libfyaml, rapidyaml, and yaml-cpp
claimed_speedup: 76.13 MiB/s vs yaml-cpp's 10.12 MiB/s (~7.5x) on ubuntu.yml; 121.04 vs 16.67 MiB/s (~7.3x) on citm_catalog.json; 56.08 vs 7.31 MiB/s (~7.7x) on citm_catalog.yml; README states 'more than 7x faster than yaml-cpp' (about 2x slower than rapidyaml on the same files)
tradeoffs: Header-only; deserializes scalars into native bool/int/double types during parsing (rather than lazily on access like yaml-cpp), which changes API ergonomics and can speed up repeated queries
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own benchmarking tool, but CPU, OS, compiler and the benchmark harness (tools/benchmark, Google Benchmark) are all fully disclosed and reproducible, meeting the Tier A bar; not yet independently reproduced by a third party

name: libfyaml
workload: Same third-party benchmark suite as the fkYAML entry (ubuntu.yml, citm_catalog.json/yml), measuring libfyaml's processed bytes/sec against yaml-cpp on identical hardware/compiler
claimed_speedup: 35.98 MiB/s vs yaml-cpp's 10.12 MiB/s (~3.6x) on ubuntu.yml; 50.71 vs 16.67 MiB/s (~3.0x) on citm_catalog.json; 21.94 vs 7.31 MiB/s (~3.0x) on citm_catalog.yml (derived from page data; slower than both rapidyaml and fkYAML in the same test)
tradeoffs: C library with a C API (not C++-idiomatic); implements the full YAML spec and passes the official YAML testsuite; usable directly from C++ as a C library per the assignment's language filter
caveats: Benchmark was run by a third party (the fkYAML author/tool), not libfyaml's own repository, but uses the exact same disclosed hardware/compiler/methodology as the fkYAML Tier-A entry above, so it independently clears the Tier A bar for this specific comparison
found_via: GitHub: fktn-k/fkYAML README benchmarking section, cross-referenced while searching YAML repos

name: libsimdxml
workload: Parsing synthetic XML files (1-30MB, deep nesting up to 22 levels, attributes, entities, CDATA, comments, PIs) into a SIMD-built structural index, single-threaded, measuring MB/s and peak RSS against pugixml 1.16 (in-situ) and libxml2 DOM
claimed_speedup: 1.19x/1.15x/1.24x faster than pugixml 1.16 at 1/5/10 MB (e.g. 245.7 vs 206.3 MB/s at 1MB); roughly 8-10x faster than libxml2 DOM (245.7 vs 28.5 MB/s at 1MB; 296.5 vs 38.0 MB/s at 10MB, derived from page data); also beats Rust's quick-xml by 1.26x-1.47x in the same cross-language run
hardware: Intel Core i7-4850HQ (Haswell, 2013 laptop), fixed at 2.3GHz base clock with turbo off for the headline speed table (a separate reference table notes a ~3.3GHz turbo-on run, explicitly not to be mixed with the base-clock numbers)
tradeoffs: Runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX2/SSE4.2/NEON/scalar all compiled into one binary, selected via [[gnu::target]]); structure-of-arrays index instead of per-node heap allocation; does not target HTML; excludes tinyxml2 and fast-xml-parser from its cross-language table because they error out on the benchmark's processing-instruction corpus
caveats: Extraordinarily detailed methodology (fixed base clock, cold-run discards, median-of-9 reps, reproducible deterministic-seed generator, explicit wall/CPU/memory separation) but the CPU model, while stated, is never paired with a stated compiler name/version or optimization flags anywhere in the README, so per the hard rules (all three of code/compiler/hardware must be stated for Tier A) this is capped at C; zero GitHub stars and unreviewed by any third party
found_via: WebSearch: "XML parser C++ 'faster than' pugixml OR libxml2 benchmark github 2025" -> KrzysztofKowalski/libsimdxml

name: RapidXml
workload: DOM parse of synthetic wide/shallow and deep/narrow XML files at sizes from 1KB to 100MB, each library in its own Docker container on a GitHub Actions runner, measuring wall time/throughput/memory/CPU (bemayer/xml-benchmark cross-language shootout, 14 libraries across 7 languages)
claimed_speedup: RapidXml throughput of 1084.9 MB/s vs libxml2's 278.8 MB/s (~3.9x) at 10MB; 638.2 vs 161.2 MB/s (~4.0x) at 100MB; 2017.2 vs 3277.1 MB/s at 100KB where libxml2 is actually faster at that size (derived from page data) -- RapidXml consistently beats libxml2 at 10MB+ but not always at small sizes, and does not beat pugixml at any size in this suite
compiler_and_flags: g++ via CMake Release build (per benchmarks/rapidxml/CMakeLists.txt: `cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`); exact flags/version not published in the report
hardware: ubuntu-latest GitHub Actions runner (exact CPU model not published)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars on this GitHub host of the code; the library itself is widely embedded/vendored (used as the RapidXml reference implementation in multiple independent XML-parser shootouts, e.g. bemayer/xml-benchmark and the SpeedyXml-cpp benchmark)
tradeoffs: In-situ, destructive parser (mutates the source buffer); allocates DOM nodes from an internal per-instance pool, which becomes a scaling bottleneck at large file sizes versus newer arena/SoA designs (see libsimdxml and parshred entries, both of which cite this exact weakness); C++03-era single-header code with no active upstream maintainer since the 1.13 release (2009); canonical home is SourceForge (http://rapidxml.sourceforge.net/), this GitHub repo is a maintained third-party host of the original source
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark suite (not RapidXml's own repo) shows it beating libxml2 by ~4x at 10MB/100MB, but the suite also shows RapidXml losing to pugixml at every size tested -- only libxml2 should be cited as the beaten baseline here, not pugixml; hardware is a generic CI runner (no CPU model stated), which caps the tier at B rather than A; the original project has had no upstream release since 2009, only community forks/mirrors remain active
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fast xml parser" -> WebSearch "XML parser C++ faster than pugixml OR libxml2 benchmark github 2025" -> bemayer/xml-benchmark shootout (gh-pages index.html data)

name: PipeYAML
workload: Load/Dump/Roundtrip/Build-sequence/Build-map microbenchmarks (Google Benchmark) on medium (~75 line), complex (anchors/aliases), and deeply-nested YAML documents, plus cached scalar type conversion, comparing against yaml-cpp 0.8
claimed_speedup: Load: 9.4x-10.5x faster (e.g. 14.3us vs yaml-cpp's 150us on a medium document); Dump: 5.0x-5.3x faster; Roundtrip (load->modify->dump): 7.5x faster; cached int/double conversion: 34x/54x faster
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.4, C++17 (exact optimization flags beyond the language standard are not stated)
tradeoffs: Type-conversion caching (int/double/bool cached on first access, O(1) subsequent reads) trades a bit of memory/complexity for large gains on repeated field access; API intentionally mirrors yaml-cpp's Node interface for easy migration
caveats: The repo's own description states the code was written by AI ('本项目代码由AI编写'), which the assignment's process calls for surfacing honestly; CPU is given only as the generic "Intel Xeon" family with no model number and no explicit compiler flags beyond -std=c++17, so this is capped at Tier C; zero stars, no evidence of external review or adoption yet
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than yaml-cpp" (zhaoliangcn/PipeYAML)

name: SpeedyXml (SpeedyXml-cpp)
workload: Single-core, streaming SAX-style push parse of a 235 MiB real-world XML document, comparing wall-clock time against pugixml (DOM), RapidXml (in-situ DOM), libxml2 (SAX2 streaming), and Expat (streaming); repeated across 8 additional public XML datasets via a bundled script
claimed_speedup: 0.34s vs libxml2's 1.53s on the 235MiB document (~4.4x faster, both streaming parsers); also faster than the DOM parsers pugixml (2.9x) and RapidXml (3.7x), though the author notes those two are not directly comparable since they hold the whole document in memory; ~680 MiB/s overall; author states 'no other parser reaches half of SpeedyXml's throughput' across the public dataset set
tradeoffs: Streaming SAX-like push model only, not a DOM (caller must build any tree themselves); does not support XML entity declarations with internal DTD subsets, no namespace resolution, UTF-8-only, requires a little-endian machine
caveats: No CPU model or compiler/flags are disclosed in the README, despite the benchmark being reproducible from source (`cmake -DBUILD_BENCHMARK=ON`, `./bench <file>`, plus tools/public_bench.sh for public datasets); the pugixml/RapidXml comparisons are DOM-vs-streaming and explicitly flagged by the author as not fully apples-to-apples, so the libxml2 comparison (both streaming) is the fairer evidence cited here; very new, low-star project with no third-party corroboration
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than libxml2" (tcShadowWalker/SpeedyXml-cpp)

name: Parshred
workload: Single-threaded DOM parse of XML files from 64KB to 128MB (bench/bench_dom, median of repeated runs), measuring MB/s and comparing against RapidXml and pugixml on the same reference machine
claimed_speedup: vs pugixml: 2572 vs 1465 MB/s (~1.76x) at 64KB; 2722 vs 821 MB/s (~3.3x) at 1MB; 2519 vs 1585 MB/s (~1.59x) at 16MB; 1678 vs 641 MB/s (~2.6x) at 64MB; 1317 vs 712 MB/s (~1.85x) at 128MB (derived from page data); vs RapidXml: within ~5% at 64KB-16MB, 1.5x-1.83x faster at 64MB+ (up to 2.4x observed on other machines per the README)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; new project (created July 2026); also ships a PyPI package (pip install parshred)
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 is a strong copyleft license (network-use/source-disclosure clause), a much bigger adoption barrier than pugixml's or RapidXml's permissive licenses; 32-byte compact DOM node format trades some API flexibility for ~3x lower memory than traditional per-node allocation; author explicitly states the large-file speedup ratio is machine-dependent (observed 1.5x-2.4x range)
caveats: First-party benchmark, but methodology is fully disclosed (exact CPU, thread count, compiler, optimization flags, and a reproducible bench binary shipped in the repo), which clears the Tier A bar per the hard rules; not yet reproduced by any independent third party; very new and unstarred so far
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "xml parser" language:C++ --sort updated (gregghy/parshred)
